questions.question_text:
Consider the following C code segment:

a = b + c;

e = a + 1;

d = b + c;

f = d + 1;

g = e + f;

In a compiler, this code segment is represented internally as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The number of nodes of nodes in the DAG is ______
questions.explanation:
To determine the number of nodes in the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representation of the given code segment, we'll step through each line and construct the DAG while identifying common subexpressions.

Given C Code Segment:

a = b + c;

e = a + 1;

d = b + c;

f = d + 1;

g = e + f;

Step-by-Step Construction:

1. Construct Nodes for Variables and Constants:

Variables: b, c

Constants: 1

2. Process Each Assignment:

Assignment 1: a = b + c;

Operation Node: + (with operands b and c)

Label: Node labeled with a

Assignment 2: e = a + 1;

Since a is b + c, we can reuse the existing + node for b + c.

Operation Node: + (with operands a (which is b + c) and 1)

Label: Node labeled with e

Assignment 3: d = b + c;

Common Subexpression: b + c already exists (from Assignment 1)

Label Addition: Node for b + c now also labeled with d

Assignment 4: f = d + 1;

Since d is b + c, we can reuse the node for b + c.

Operation Node: + (with operands d (which is b + c) and 1)

Common Subexpression: d + 1 is the same as a + 1 which we have labeled as e

Label Addition: Node for a + 1 now also labeled with f

Assignment 5: g = e + f;

Since e and f are both a + 1 (which is (b + c) + 1), they point to the same node.

Operation Node: + (with operands e and f which are the same node)

Label: Node labeled with g

DAG Representation:

Node 1: b (variable)

Node 2: c (variable)

Node 3: + operation with operands b and c; labeled with a and d

Node 4: 1 (constant)

Node 5: + operation with operands Node 3 (b + c) and Node 4 (1); labeled with e and f

Node 6: + operation with operands Node 5 ((b + c) + 1) and Node 5 (since e and f are the same); labeled with g

Counting the Nodes:

Total Nodes: 6

Therefore, the number of nodes in the DAG is 6.

Answer: 6

questions.question_text:
A lexical analyzer uses the following patterns to recognize three tokens $${T_1},{T_2},$$ and $${T_3}$$ over the alphabet $$\left\{ {a,b,c} \right\}.$$

$$\eqalign{ & {T_1}:\,\,\,a?{\left( {b|c} \right)^ * }a \cr & {T_2}:\,\,\,b?{\left( {a|c} \right)^ * }b \cr & {T_3}:\,\,\,c?{\left( {b|a} \right)^ * }c \cr} $$

Note that $$'x?'$$ means $$0$$ or $$1$$ occurrence of the symbol $$x.$$ Note also that the analyzer outputs the token that matches the longest possible prefix.

If the string $$bbaacabc$$ is processed by the analyzer, which one of the following is the sequence of tokens it outputs?
questions.explanation:
The lexical analyzer processes the input string bbaacabc by repeatedly finding the longest prefix that matches any of the given token patterns $T_1, T_2, T_3$.

The token patterns are:

  • $T_1: a? (b|c)^* a$

  • $T_2: b? (a|c)^* b$

  • $T_3: c? (b|a)^* c$

Let's break down the processing:

Step 1: Process bbaacabc

We will look for the longest prefix of bbaacabc that matches $T_1$, $T_2$, or $T_3$.

  • For $T_1: a? (b|c)^* a$

    This pattern requires the string to end with 'a'. The part before the final 'a' must be optional 'a' followed by zero or more 'b's or 'c's.

    • bba: Matches $T_1$. (Optional a? is empty, (b|c)^* matches bb, final a matches a). Length = 3.

    • bbaa: Does not match. The last a is the final a. The prefix bba does not match a?(b|c)^* because bba contains an a which is not at the start and not allowed in (b|c)^*.

    • bbaaca: Does not match. The last a is the final a. The prefix bbaac does not match a?(b|c)^* because bbaac contains an a which is not at the start and not allowed in (b|c)^*.

    • No other longer prefixes ending in a match $T_1$.

    • Longest $T_1$ match: bba (Length 3)

  • For $T_2: b? (a|c)^* b$

    This pattern requires the string to end with 'b'. The part before the final 'b' must be optional 'b' followed by zero or more 'a's or 'c's.

    • b: Matches $T_2$. (Optional b? is empty, (a|c)^* matches empty string, final b matches b). Length = 1.

    • bb: Matches $T_2$. (Optional b? matches b, (a|c)^* matches empty string, final b matches b). Length = 2.

    • bbaacab: Does not match. The last b is the final b. The prefix bbaaca must match b?(a|c)^*.

      • If b? is empty: bbaaca does not match (a|c)^* as it contains b.

      • If b? matches b: bbaaca must match b(a|c)^*. The b matches first b. The baaca does not match (a|c)^* as it contains b.

    • Longest $T_2$ match: bb (Length 2)

  • For $T_3: c? (b|a)^* c$

    This pattern requires the string to end with 'c'. The part before the final 'c' must be optional 'c' followed by zero or more 'b's or 'a's.

    • bbaac: Matches $T_3$. (Optional c? is empty, (b|a)^* matches bbaa, final c matches c). Length = 5.

    • bbaacabc: Does not match. The last c is the final c. The prefix bbaacab must match c?(b|a)^*.

      • If c? is empty: bbaacab does not match (b|a)^* as it contains c.

      • If c? matches c: bbaacab must match c(b|a)^*. It does not start with c.

    • Longest $T_3$ match: bbaac (Length 5)

Comparing the longest matches:

  • $T_1$: bba (Length 3)

  • $T_2$: bb (Length 2)

  • $T_3$: bbaac (Length 5)

The longest prefix is bbaac, which matches $T_3$.

Output: $T_3$.

Remaining string: abc.

Step 2: Process abc

We will look for the longest prefix of abc that matches $T_1$, $T_2$, or $T_3$.

  • For $T_1: a? (b|c)^* a$

    • a: Matches $T_1$. (Optional a? is empty, (b|c)^* matches empty string, final a matches a). Length = 1.

    • Longest $T_1$ match: a (Length 1)

  • For $T_2: b? (a|c)^* b$

    • ab: Matches $T_2$. (Optional b? is empty, (a|c)^* matches a, final b matches b). Length = 2.

    • Longest $T_2$ match: ab (Length 2)

  • For $T_3: c? (b|a)^* c$

    • abc: Matches $T_3$. (Optional c? is empty, (b|a)^* matches ab, final c matches c). Length = 3.

    • Longest $T_3$ match: abc (Length 3)

Comparing the longest matches:

  • $T_1$: a (Length 1)

  • $T_2$: ab (Length 2)

  • $T_3$: abc (Length 3)

The longest prefix is abc, which matches $T_3$.

Output: $T_3$.

Remaining string: empty.

The sequence of tokens outputted is $T_3 T_3$.

The final answer is $\boxed{\text{${T_3}{T_3}$}}$.

questions.explanation:
Let's analyze each option:

Option A: For a production $$A \rightarrow \varepsilon,$$ $$\varepsilon$$ is added to $$\text{FIRST}(A)$$.

Option B: If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to $$\text{FIRST}(S)$$, where $$S$$ is the start symbol.

questions.explanation:
Let's analyze each option to see which one is false:

Option A: "Symbol table is responsible for keeping track of the scope of variables."

This is true. The symbol table maintains details about identifiers, including their scope and type, which is essential during semantic analysis and later stages.

Option B: "Symbol table can be implemented using a binary search tree."

This is also true. Although hash tables are common, one can indeed implement a symbol table with a binary search tree.

Option C: "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase."

This is false. The symbol table is crucial not just during parsing but also in subsequent phases such as semantic analysis, type checking, and code generation.

Option D: "Symbol table is created during the lexical analysis phase."

This statement can be considered true in many implementations. Often, the lexical analyzer initializes or interacts with an identifier table (sometimes considered part of the overall symbol table) when it recognizes identifiers, although the complete information might be filled in later.

Since only one statement is false, the answer is:

$$\textbf{Option C is false}$$

questions.question_text: Which of the following is/are Bottom-Up Parser(s)?
questions.explanation:
To answer this question, let's first understand the difference between Bottom-Up and Top-Down parsers. This understanding will help us to identify which of the given options are Bottom-Up parsers.

Bottom-Up Parsing: In bottom-up parsing, the parser starts with the input symbols and tries to construct the parse tree up to the start symbol. Essentially, the parsing process begins from the leaves (i.e., the input symbols) and works its way up to the root (i.e., the start symbol of the grammar). The key examples of bottom-up parsers are:

  • Shift-Reduce Parser: This is a type of bottom-up parser that uses a stack to hold symbols and applies reductions to convert a sequence of symbols into a higher-level non-terminal symbol until the start symbol is derived.
  • LR Parser: This is a more powerful bottom-up parser that can handle a broad class of grammars, including all deterministic context-free grammars. It includes variations such as SLR (Simple LR), LALR (Look-Ahead LR), and Canonical LR parsers.

Top-Down Parsing: In contrast, top-down parsing starts with the start symbol and tries to derive the input symbols by breaking down the non-terminals to the terminals. Examples of top-down parsers include:

  • Predictive Parser: This is a type of top-down parser which uses lookahead to decide which production to apply, and generally avoids backtracking. LL(1) parser is a specific type of predictive parser.
  • LL(1) Parser: This is a type of top-down parser where the first 'L' stands for scanning the input from left to right, the second 'L' stands for producing a leftmost derivation, and '1' stands for using one lookahead symbol.

Given the options:

  • Option A: Shift-reduce Parser - This is a bottom-up parser.
  • Option B: Predictive Parser - This is a top-down parser.
  • Option C: LL(1) Parser - This is a top-down parser.
  • Option D: LR Parser - This is a bottom-up parser.

Based on these explanations, the bottom-up parsers among the given options are:

  • Option A: Shift-reduce Parser
  • Option D: LR Parser

Therefore, the correct answers are Option A and Option D.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following grammar $G$, with $S$ as the start symbol. The grammar $G$ has three incomplete productions denoted by (1), (2), and (3).

$$S \rightarrow d a T \mid \underline{\ (1)}$$

$$T \rightarrow a S \mid b T \mid \ \underline{(2)}$$

$$R \rightarrow \underline{(3)} \mid \epsilon$$

The set of terminals is $\{a, b, c, d, f\}$. The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different non-terminals are as follows.

FIRST($S$) = $\{c, d, f\}$, FIRST($T$) = $\{a, b, \epsilon\}$, FIRST($R$) = $\{c, \epsilon\}$

FOLLOW($S$) = FOLLOW($T$) = $\{c, f, \#\}$, FOLLOW($R$) = $\{f\}$

Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete productions?

options.content: (1) $S \rightarrow f R$ (2) $T \rightarrow c T$ (3) $R \rightarrow c R$
(1) $S \rightarrow R f$ (2) $T \rightarrow c T$ (3) $R \rightarrow c R$

questions.explanation:
To determine the correct productions that fill in the incomplete parts of the grammar, we need to ensure that the provided FIRST and FOLLOW sets are consistent with the production rules. Let's analyze each option based on the provided FIRST and FOLLOW sets.

Option A:

(1) $$S \rightarrow R f$$
(2) $$T \rightarrow \epsilon$$
(3) $$R \rightarrow c T R$$

Let's verify each production:

  • For (1) $$S \rightarrow R f$$, we need to check if this rule will maintain the FIRST($S$) = {c, d, f}. Since FIRST($R$) = {c, $\epsilon$}, the FIRST set of $$R f$$ can be {c, f}. Hence, this is consistent with FIRST($S$).

  • For (2) $$T \rightarrow \epsilon$$, it is consistent with the given FIRST($T$) = {a, b, $\epsilon$}.

  • For (3) $$R \rightarrow c T R$$, FIRST($R$) should include c, which it does. The production can generate strings starting with c, followed by strings derived from TR. It matches the condition that FIRST($R$) contains c.

The FOLLOW sets are also checked:

  • FOLLOW($S$) = FOLLOW($T$) = {c, f, #}, and FOLLOW($R$) = {f}. The non-terminal $R$ in $$S \rightarrow R f$$ should respect FOLLOW($R$) = f.

Option A appears consistent with the given FIRST and FOLLOW sets.

Option B:

(1) $$S \rightarrow f R$$
(2) $$T \rightarrow \epsilon$$
(3) $$R \rightarrow c T R$$

Let's verify each production:

  • For (1) $$S \rightarrow f R$$, FIRST($S$) should include f, which is consistent with given FIRST($S$) = {c, d, f}.

  • For (2) $$T \rightarrow \epsilon$$, it matches the FIRST($T$) = {a, b, $\epsilon$}.

  • For (3) $$R \rightarrow c T R$$, this maintains the FIRST($R$) = {c, $\epsilon$}.

Option B appears consistent with the given FIRST and FOLLOW sets.

Option C:

(1) $$S \rightarrow f R$$
(2) $$T \rightarrow c T$$
(3) $$R \rightarrow c R$$

Let's verify each production:

  • For (1) $$S \rightarrow f R$$, it maintains FIRST($S$) = {c, d, f}.

  • For (2) $$T \rightarrow c T$$, this would mean FIRST($T$) = {c}, which is not consistent with the given FIRST($T$) = {a, b, $\epsilon$}.

  • For (3) $$R \rightarrow c R$$, this would mean FIRST($R$) = {c}, but it should also include epsilon as given.

Option C is inconsistent with the given FIRST sets.

Option D:

(1) $$S \rightarrow R f$$
(2) $$T \rightarrow c T$$
(3) $$R \rightarrow c R$$

Let's verify each production:

  • For (1) $$S \rightarrow R f$$, it maintains FIRST($S$) = {c, d, f}.

  • For (2) $$T \rightarrow c T$$, it sets FIRST($T$) = {c}, which is not consistent with the given FIRST($T$) = {a, b, $\epsilon$}.

  • For (3) $$R \rightarrow c R$$, this restricts FIRST($R$) = {c}, which does not include epsilon as required.

Option D is inconsistent with the given FIRST sets.

Therefore, the correct option that correctly fills in the incomplete productions is Option A.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.content: An attribute grammar is a syntax-directed definition (SDD) in which the functions in the semantic rules have no side effects
The attributes in a L-attributed definition cannot always be evaluated in a depth-first order
Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser as the input is parsed
All L-attributed definitions based on LR(1) grammar can be evaluated using a bottom-up parsing strategy

questions.explanation:
Let's analyze each option one by one to identify which statements are false:

Option A: An attribute grammar is a syntax-directed definition (SDD) in which the functions in the semantic rules have no side effects.

This statement is true. An attribute grammar is exactly as described: it is a form of SDD where semantic rules are purely functional and have no side effects.

Option B: The attributes in a L-attributed definition cannot always be evaluated in a depth-first order.

This statement is false. L-attributed definitions are specifically designed so that their attributes can be evaluated in a depth-first manner. Thus, the depth-first order evaluation of attributes is always possible for L-attributed definitions.

Option C: Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser as the input is parsed.

This statement is true. Synthesized attributes, by definition, depend only on the attributes of a node’s children. In bottom-up parsing, as each rule is reduced, the synthesized attributes can be evaluated, making them suitable for such parsing strategies.

Option D: All L-attributed definitions based on LR(1) grammar can be evaluated using a bottom-up parsing strategy.

This statement is false. While it's true that synthesized attributes in LR(1) grammars can often be evaluated in a bottom-up fashion, L-attributed definitions can also include inherited attributes, which require information from parent or sibling nodes and may not always be suitable for purely bottom-up parsing.

So, the statements that are FALSE are:

  • Option B
  • Option D

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements regarding the front-end and back-end of a compiler.

S1: The front-end includes phases that are independent of the target hardware.

S2: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the target hardware.

S3: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the programming language used in the source code.

Identify the CORRECT option.

options.content: Only S1 and S2 is TRUE.
S1, S2 and S3 are all TRUE.
Only S1 and S3 are TRUE.

questions.explanation:
The correct option is Option B: Only S1 and S2 are TRUE.

Here's a breakdown of why:

S1: The front-end includes phases that are independent of the target hardware.

This statement is TRUE. The front-end of a compiler deals with the source code and its translation into an intermediate representation. This process is largely independent of the target hardware. Here are some key phases of the front-end:

  • Lexical Analysis: Reading the source code character by character and grouping them into meaningful units called tokens (e.g., keywords, identifiers, operators, constants).
  • Syntax Analysis: Checking the grammatical correctness of the token sequence, ensuring it follows the rules of the programming language. This is also known as parsing.
  • Semantic Analysis: Verifying the meaning and consistency of the code. This involves type checking, ensuring variables are used appropriately, and resolving any ambiguities in the code.
  • Intermediate Code Generation: Converting the source code into an intermediate representation (IR), which is often a platform-independent language that is easier to optimize and translate into machine code.

These phases focus on understanding the source code, not on the specific architecture of the target machine.

S2: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the target hardware.

This statement is also TRUE. The back-end of a compiler is responsible for generating machine code that can run on a specific target architecture. These phases are highly dependent on the target hardware:

  • Code Optimization: Improving the efficiency and performance of the intermediate code for the target hardware. This could involve rearranging instructions, removing redundant code, and using registers effectively.
  • Code Generation: Converting the optimized intermediate code into machine code (binary instructions) that the target processor can execute.
  • Assembly: (Sometimes included in code generation) Translating the machine code into assembly language, which is a human-readable representation of the machine instructions.

The back-end needs to understand the target processor's instruction set, memory organization, and other hardware-specific details.

S3: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the programming language used in the source code.

This statement is FALSE. While the front-end is specific to the programming language (e.g., C, Python, Java), the back-end focuses on the target machine, not the specific language used in the source code. The back-end takes the intermediate code, which has already been language-independent, and translates it to machine code for the target platform. It doesn't matter if the intermediate code was generated from C, Python, or any other language.

In summary: The front-end deals with the source code and its translation to a platform-independent representation, while the back-end tailors the code for the specific hardware architecture of the target machine.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements.

S1 : Every SLR(1) grammar is unambiguous but there are certain unambiguous grammars that are not SLR(1).

S2 : For any context-free grammar, there is a parser that takes at most O(n3) time to parse a string of length n.

Which one of the following option is correct?

options.content: S<sub>1</sub> is true and S<sub>2</sub> is false
S<sub>1</sub> is false and S<sub>2</sub> is true
S<sub>1</sub> is true and S<sub>2</sub> is true
S<sub>1</sub> is false and S<sub>2</sub> is false

questions.explanation:
Statement $ S_1 $:

Every SLR(1) grammar is unambiguous but there are certain unambiguous grammars that are not SLR(1).

Analysis:

Every SLR(1) Grammar is Unambiguous

SLR(1) Grammars:

SLR(1) stands for Simple LR(1). These grammars can be parsed using SLR(1) parsers without conflicts.

SLR(1) grammars are a subset of LR(1) grammars.

Unambiguity:

LR(1) grammars are deterministic context-free grammars.

Deterministic context-free grammars are unambiguous because they produce a unique parse tree for each valid string.

Conclusion:

All SLR(1) grammars are unambiguous.

There Exist Unambiguous Grammars That Are Not SLR(1)

Unambiguous Grammars Not in SLR(1):

Not all unambiguous grammars can be parsed using SLR(1) parsing tables without conflicts.

Example:

Consider the following unambiguous grammar:

$ S \rightarrow aSa \mid bSb \mid c $

This grammar is unambiguous but not SLR(1) because it requires more lookahead to parse without conflicts.

Conclusion:

There are unambiguous grammars that are not SLR(1).

Overall Conclusion for $ S_1 $: True

Statement $ S_2 $:

For any context-free grammar, there is a parser that takes at most $ O(n^3) $ time to parse a string of length $ n $.

Analysis:

Parsing Arbitrary Context-Free Grammars:

CYK Algorithm:

The Cocke-Younger-Kasami (CYK) algorithm can parse any context-free grammar (in Chomsky Normal Form) in $ O(n^3) $ time.

Earley's Algorithm:

Earley's parser can parse any context-free grammar in $ O(n^3) $ time in the worst case.

For unambiguous grammars, Earley's parser operates in $ O(n^2) $ time, and for a large class of grammars (including LR(k) grammars), it operates in $ O(n) $ time.

Conclusion:

There exists a general parsing algorithm with $ O(n^3) $ time complexity for any context-free grammar.

Overall Conclusion for $ S_2 $: True

Final Answer:

$ S_1 $ is True

$ S_2 $ is True

Therefore, the correct choice is:

Option C: $ S_1 $ is true and $ S_2 $ is true.

Answer: Option C

questions.question_text:
Consider the productions A $$ \to $$ PQ and A $$ \to $$ XY. Each of the five non-terminals A, P, Q, X, and Y has two attributes: s is a synthesized attribute, and i is an inherited attribute. Consider the following rules.

Rule 1 : P.i = A.i + 2, Q.i = P.i + A.i, and A.s = P.s + Q.s
Rule 2 : X.i = A.i + Y.s and Y.i = X.s + A.i

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.content: Neither Rule 1 nor Rule 2 is L-attributed.
Both Rule 1 and Rule 2 are L-attributed.

questions.explanation:
To determine which of the given rules are L-attributed, we'll analyze each rule in the context of attribute grammars and the definitions of L-attributed grammars.

Understanding L-Attributed Grammars:

An attribute grammar is L-attributed if the attributes can be evaluated in a single left-to-right traversal of the parse tree. Specifically:

Inherited attributes of a symbol can depend only on:

Attributes of the parent node.

Attributes of any siblings to the left (but not to the right).

Attributes of ancestors (nodes higher up in the tree).

Synthesized attributes can depend on:

Attributes of the symbol's children.

Attributes of the symbol itself (for recursive definitions).

Key Restrictions for L-attributed grammars:

An inherited attribute cannot depend on attributes of right siblings or children.

A synthesized attribute can depend on attributes of the node's children.

Given Productions and Rules:

Production 1: $ A \to P \ Q $

Rule 1:

$ P.i = A.i + 2 $

$ Q.i = P.i + A.i $

$ A.s = P.s + Q.s $

Production 2: $ A \to X \ Y $

Rule 2:

$ X.i = A.i + Y.s $

$ Y.i = X.s + A.i $

Analyzing Rule 1:

Production: $ A \to P \ Q $

Rules:

$ P.i = A.i + 2 $

$ P.i $ is an inherited attribute of $ P $.

Depends on $ A.i $ (inherited attribute of parent $ A $), which is allowed.

Conclusion: Valid for L-attributed grammar.

$ Q.i = P.i + A.i $

$ Q.i $ is an inherited attribute of $ Q $.

Depends on:

$ P.i $ (inherited attribute of left sibling $ P $) — allowed.

$ A.i $ (inherited attribute of parent $ A $) — allowed.

Conclusion: Valid for L-attributed grammar.

$ A.s = P.s + Q.s $

$ A.s $ is a synthesized attribute of $ A $.

Depends on $ P.s $ and $ Q.s $ (synthesized attributes of children) — allowed.

Conclusion: Valid for L-attributed grammar.

Overall Conclusion for Rule 1: All dependencies comply with L-attributed restrictions.

Analyzing Rule 2:

Production: $ A \to X \ Y $

Rules:

$ X.i = A.i + Y.s $

$ X.i $ is an inherited attribute of $ X $.

Depends on:

$ A.i $ (inherited attribute of parent $ A $) — allowed.

$ Y.s $ (synthesized attribute of right sibling $ Y $) — NOT allowed in L-attributed grammars.

Violation: Inherited attribute depending on the synthesized attribute of a right sibling is not permitted.

Conclusion: Rule violates L-attributed restrictions.

$ Y.i = X.s + A.i $

$ Y.i $ is an inherited attribute of $ Y $.

Depends on:

$ X.s $ (synthesized attribute of left sibling $ X $) — allowed.

$ A.i $ (inherited attribute of parent $ A $) — allowed.

Conclusion: Valid for L-attributed grammar.

Overall Conclusion for Rule 2: **Rule 2 is *not* L-attributed due to the dependency of $ X.i $ on $ Y.s $.**

Final Answer:

Rule 1 is L-attributed.

Rule 2 is not L-attributed.

Answer: Option D

Only Rule 1 is L-attributed.

Consider the augmented grammar given below :

S' → S
S → 〈L〉 | id
L → L,S | S

Let I0 = CLOSURE ({[S' → ●S]}). The number of items in the set GOTO (I0 , 〈 ) is: _____.
questions.explanation:
Given Grammar :

Augmented Grammar :

$ \begin{align*} S' &\to S \\ S &\to \langle L \rangle \mid \text{id} \\ L &\to L, S \mid S \end{align*} $

Initial Item Set $ I_0 $ :

$ I_0 = \text{CLOSURE}(\{ [S' \to \bullet S] \}) $

Step 1 : Compute $ I_0 $

Starting with $ [S' \to \bullet S] $ :

Since the dot is before $ S $, and $ S $ is a non-terminal, we add items for all productions of $ S $ :

$ [S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle] $

$ [S \to \bullet \text{id}] $

The symbols after the dots are terminals ($ \langle $ and $ \text{id} $), so no further closure is needed.

Items in $ I_0 $:

$ [S' \to \bullet S] $

$ [S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle] $

$ [S \to \bullet \text{id}] $

Step 2: Compute $ \text{GOTO}(I_0, \langle) $

Identify items in $ I_0 $ where the dot is before $ \langle $:

$ [S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle] $

Shift over $ \langle $:

$ [S \to \langle \bullet L \rangle] $

Compute the closure starting from this item:

Add the initial item:

$ [S \to \langle \bullet L \rangle] $

Since the dot is before $ L $ (a non-terminal), add items for $ L $:

$ [L \to \bullet L, S] $

$ [L \to \bullet S] $

**In $ [L \to \bullet L, S] $, the dot is before $ L $, so we need items for $ L $ again. However, these items are already included, so we stop here.

In $ [L \to \bullet S] $, the dot is before $ S $, add items for $ S $:

$ [S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle] $

$ [S \to \bullet \text{id}] $

No further closure is needed as the dots are before terminals or already included non-terminals.

Items in $ \text{GOTO}(I_0, \langle) $:

$ [S \to \langle \bullet L \rangle] $

$ [L \to \bullet L, S] $

SDD1
Grammar(G1) $$

$$		 $$

& \text { D.type = T.type } \\
& \text { V.type = T.type }
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\mathrm{T} \rightarrow \mathrm{int}
$$		 $$
\text { T.type = int }
$$
$$

$$		 $$
\text { T.type = float }
$$
$$

$$		 $$
\begin{aligned}
& V_1 \cdot \text { type }=\text { V.type } \\

\end{aligned}
$$
$$

$$		 $$
\text { put(id.entry, V.type) }
$$
SDD2
Grammar(G2) $$
\text { Semantic Rules }
$$
$$
\mathrm{D} \rightarrow D_1 \mathrm{id}
$$		 $$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { D.type }=D_1 \cdot \text { type } \\
& \text { put(id.entry, } D_1 \cdot \text { type) }
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{~T} \text { id }
$$		 $$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { D.type = T.type } \\
& \text { put(id.entry, T.type) }
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\mathrm{T} \rightarrow \text { int }
$$		 $$
\text { T.type = int }
$$
$$
\mathrm{T} \rightarrow \text { float }
$$		 $$
\text { T.type = float }
$$
$D$ is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal $V_1$ is the same as $V$ and the non-terminal $D_1$ is the same as $D$. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the languages specified by grammars G1 and G2, respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.content: The languages P and Q are the same
SDD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes
SDD1 is L-attributed and contains only inherited attributes
The specifications of SDD1 and SDD2 are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table

questions.explanation:
(a) True: Both the grammars generate the same language, that is, declarations of the form $$ (\text{int} \; / \; \text{float}) \; (\text{id})^{+} $$ This means one type name is followed by one or more identifiers.

In SDD1, the grammar is $$ D \rightarrow TV $$ where $$ T \rightarrow \text{int} \; | \; \text{float} $$ and $$ V \rightarrow V_1 \; \text{id} \; | \; \text{id} $$ So, after choosing a type, we get one or more identifiers.

In SDD2 also, the grammar gives the same form. Here, identifiers are built using $$ D \rightarrow D_1 \; \text{id} $$ and the base case is $$ D \rightarrow T \; \text{id} $$ Therefore, this grammar also generates one type followed by one or more identifiers. So, $$ P = Q $$.

(c) False: SDD1 is not S-attributed. It is L-attributed because it uses both synthesized and inherited attributes.

In SDD1, $$ T.type $$ is synthesized from $$ T $$. Then this type is passed from $$ D $$ to $$ V $$ using $$ V.type = T.type $$. After that, in the production $$ V \rightarrow V_1 \; \text{id} $$, the rule $$ V_1.type = V.type $$ passes the type information downwards. This is an inherited attribute.

Since inherited attributes are used in SDD1, it cannot be S-attributed. Therefore, statement (c) is false.

(b) True: SDD2 is S-attributed because it uses only synthesized attributes.

In SDD2, the rules are:

$$ T.type = \text{int} \quad \text{or} \quad T.type = \text{float} $$

Then, in $$ D \rightarrow T \; \text{id} $$, we get $$ D.type = T.type $$, and in $$ D \rightarrow D_1 \; \text{id} $$, we get $$ D.type = D_1.type $$.

Here, type information always moves upward from child to parent. No attribute is passed from parent to child or from left to right. So, only synthesized attributes are used. Hence SDD2 is S-attributed.

(d) True: Both SDD1 and SDD2 make the same symbol table entries.

In SDD1, after the type is known, every identifier in $$ V $$ gets entered into the symbol table using $$ \text{put}(\text{id.entry}, V.type) $$.

In SDD2 also, each identifier is entered using either $$ \text{put}(\text{id.entry}, T.type) $$ or $$ \text{put}(\text{id.entry}, D_1.type) $$. Since $$ D_1.type $$ is ultimately the same type obtained from $$ T $$, all identifiers receive the same correct type.

So, for any valid declaration, both SDD1 and SDD2 insert exactly the same identifier-type pairs into the symbol table.

∴ (a), (b), (d) are true and (c) is false.

questions.question_text:
Given the following syntax directed translation rules :

Rule 1 : $R \rightarrow A B\{B . i=R . i-1 ; A . i=B . i R . i=A . i+1 ;\}$

Rule 2 : $P \rightarrow C D\{P . i=C . i+D . i ; D . i=C . i+2\}$

Rule 3 : $Q \rightarrow E F\{Q . i=E . i+F . i ;\}$

Which ONE is the CORRECT option among the following?

options.content: Rule 1 is S -attributed and L-attributed; Rule 2 is S -attributed and not L-attributed; Rule 3 is neither S -attributed nor L-attributed
Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed: Rule 2 is S-attributed and L-attributed: Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed
Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed; Rule 2 is not S -attributed and is Lattributed; Rule 3 is S -attributed and L-attributed
Rule 1 is S-attributed and not L-attributed; Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is Lattributed: Rule 3 is S -attributed and L-attributed

questions.explanation:
Let’s analyze each rule step by step.

──────────────────────────────

Rule 1:

$$ R \rightarrow A \; B \; \{\, B.i = R.i - 1;\quad A.i = B.i;\quad R.i = A.i + 1;\,\} $$

• In this rule, the first action sets

$$ B.i = R.i - 1. $$

That means the attribute for B is computed from a value in the parent (R), which makes it an inherited attribute. (Recall: an S‑attributed grammar uses only synthesized attributes and does not compute values from the parent.)

• The next action is

$$ A.i = B.i. $$

Now, note that A appears to the left of B in the production. In an L‑attributed grammar, any inherited attribute of a symbol can depend only on the inherited attributes of the parent and on the attributes of symbols already processed to its left. Here, A’s attribute is computed using B’s attribute—even though B is to the right of A. This is not allowed in L‑attributed definitions.

Thus, Rule 1 involves an inherited attribute and violates the left-to-right condition; it is neither S‑attributed (because S‑attributed grammars allow only synthesized attributes) nor L‑attributed.

──────────────────────────────

    Rule 2:

    $$ P \rightarrow C \; D \; \{\, P.i = C.i + D.i; \quad D.i = C.i + 2;\,\} $$

    • Here, the action

    $$ D.i = C.i + 2 $$

    computes an attribute for D using the attribute of C. Since C appears to the left of D in the production, this dependency is acceptable for an L‑attributed grammar (inherited attributes are allowed to depend on the left siblings and on attributes from the parent).

    • However, because the rule assigns an attribute value to D (which is computed from a left sibling rather than solely from information in its own subtree), it is not purely synthesized. In S‑attributed grammars only synthesized attributes are allowed, so this rule is not S‑attributed.

    Thus, Rule 2 is not S‑attributed but is L‑attributed.

    ──────────────────────────────

      Rule 3:

      $$ Q \rightarrow E \; F \; \{\, Q.i = E.i + F.i; \,\} $$

      • In this rule, the only semantic action computes

      $$ Q.i = E.i + F.i. $$

      This uses only the attributes of the children E and F to compute the synthesized attribute for Q.

      Since no inherited attribute is used, this rule is S‑attributed. (And every S‑attributed rule is trivially L‑attributed as well.)

      ──────────────────────────────

      Summary of classifications:

      • Rule 1 is neither S‑attributed (because it uses parent's attribute to compute a child’s attribute) nor L‑attributed (because it uses a right sibling’s attribute to compute an attribute for an earlier symbol).

      • Rule 2 is not S‑attributed (inherited computation is present) but is L‑attributed (dependencies are only on the parent and left sibling).

      • Rule 3 is S‑attributed (and hence also L‑attributed).

      ──────────────────────────────

      Thus, the correct option is:

      Option C

      ──────────────────────────────

      Final answer: Option C.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for

(I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass.

(II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass.

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
Backpatching is a technique where jump addresses are left unspecified and later “patched” once the target addresses are known. This is particularly useful in a one-pass compiler for handling constructs that involve jumps, such as Boolean expressions and flow-of-control statements.

Here's how it applies to both statements:

$$\textbf{Boolean Expressions:}$$

When translating Boolean expressions (especially those with short-circuit behavior), we often create lists for true and false jump addresses.

Backpatching lets us fill in these addresses later, once the complete control flow is determined.

This allows the code for Boolean expressions to be generated in one pass.

$$\textbf{Flow-of-Control Statements:}$$

Statements like if, while, and for involve jumps to different parts of the code.

By using backpatching, the compiler can defer specifying the jump targets until it has processed the entire structure of the statement.

This, too, enables one-pass code generation for these constructs.

Since backpatching serves both purposes:

Statement (I) is correct.

Statement (II) is also correct.

Thus, the correct answer is:

Option C: Both (I) and (II) are correct.

Consider the following syntax-directed definition (SDD).
S → DHTU { S.val = D.val + H.val + T.val + U.val; }
D → “M” D1 { D.val = 5 + D1.val; }
D → ε { D.val = –5; }
H → “L” H1 { H.val = 5 * 10 + H1.val; }
H → ε { H.val = –10; }
T → “C” T1 { T.val = 5 * 100 + T1.val; }
T → ε { T.val = –5; }
U → “K” { U.val = 5; }
Given “MMLK” as the input, which one of the following options is the CORRECT value computed by the SDD (in the attribute S.val)?
questions.explanation:
To calculate the value of the attribute $$S.val$$ for the input string "MMLK", we will use the given syntax-directed definition (SDD) rules step by step.

1. Parsing the input "MMLK":

  • S → DHTU
  • D → “M” D1
  • D1 → “M” D2
  • D2 → ε
  • H → “L” H1
  • H1 → ε
  • T → ε
  • U → “K”

2. Applying the semantic rules:

  • Starting from the innermost $$D$$ production: $$D_2$$

    $$D_2.val = -5$$ as $$D_2 → ε$$

  • Moving one level up to $$D_1$$:

    $$D_1.val = 5 + D_2.val = 5 + (-5) = 0$$ as $$D_1 → “M” D_2$$

  • Then up to $$D$$:

    $$D.val = 5 + D_1.val = 5 + 0 = 5$$ as $$D → “M” D_1$$

  • For $$H₁$$:

    $$H_1.val = -10$$ as $$H_1 → ε$$

  • Then $$H$$:

    $$H.val = 5 * 10 + H_1.val = 50 + (-10) = 40$$ as $$H → “L” H_1$$

  • For $$T$$:

    $$T.val = -5$$ as $$T → ε$$

  • For $$U$$:

    $$U.val = 5$$ as $$U → “K”$$

Finally, combining all these values for $$S$$:

$$S.val = D.val + H.val + T.val + U.val = 5 + 40 + (-5) + 5 = 45$$

Thus, the correct value computed by the SDD for the input "MMLK" is:

Option A: 45

questions.question_text:
Consider the following expression: $x[i] = (p + r) * -s[i] + \frac{u}{w}$. The following sequence shows the list of triples representing the given expression, with entries missing for triples (1), (3), and (6).

(0) + p r
(1)
(2) uminus (1)
(3)
(4) / u w
(5) + (3)(4)
(6)
(7) = (6)(5)

Which one of the following options fills in the missing entries CORRECTLY?
questions.explanation:
Let's break down the given expression x[i] = (p + r) * -s[i] + u/w and fill in the missing triples following the common structure (result_register) operator operand1 operand2.

  1. p + r:

    The triple (0) + p r correctly computes p + r. Let's denote its result as t0. So, t0 = p + r.

  2. s[i]:

    The expression needs -s[i], so s[i] must be fetched first. This value will be stored in (1).

    Looking at the options for (1):

    • = [] s i: This implies an assignment (=) where the right-hand side [] s i means "fetch array s at index i." So (1) gets s[i]. This is a plausible interpretation of the syntax.

    • []= s i: This typically means "store to array." If (1) is the result register, this syntax ((1) []= s i) is unusual for fetching a value, as []= usually takes a value to store as well.

  3. -s[i]:

    The triple (2) uminus (1) computes the unary minus of (1). If (1) holds s[i], then (2) holds -s[i]. Let t2 = -s[i].

  4. (p + r) * -s[i]:

    This is (0) * (2). This value will be stored in (3).

    Looking at the options for (3):

    • * (0) (2): This correctly computes (0) * (2). This matches the expression and is standard triple syntax.

    • - (0) (2): This computes (0) - (2), which is incorrect as we need multiplication.

    Therefore, (3) * (0) (2) is the correct operation. Let t3 = (p + r) * -s[i]. This eliminates options B and D.

  5. u / w:

    The triple (4) / u w correctly computes u / w. Let t4 = u / w.

  6. (p + r) * -s[i] + u/w:

    The triple (5) + (3) (4) correctly computes (3) + (4). This sums the product part and the division part. (5) now holds the complete right-hand side of the expression. Let t5 = (p + r) * -s[i] + u/w.

  7. x[i] = RHS:

    The final expression is an assignment to x[i]. The value to be assigned is (5). The assignment instruction is given by (7) = (6) (5).

    This triple (7) = (6) (5) follows the pattern (destination) = (source). It means the value (5) is assigned to the destination represented by (6).

    Therefore, (6) must represent the assignable location x[i].

    Now let's compare Option A and C for (1) and (6):

    Option A:

    • (1) = [] s i: As interpreted before, (1) is assigned the result of [] s i, which is s[i]. So t1 = s[i]. This makes (2) uminus (1) work correctly.

    • (6) []= x i: This triple defines (6). If (6) needs to represent the assignable location x[i], then []= x i means "reference to x[i]" or "address of x[i]" (L-value). This is a plausible specific notation. So, t6 is the L-value for x[i].

    • (7) = (6) (5): This means assign (5) (R-value) to (6) (L-value), effectively x[i] = t5.

    Option C:

    • (1) =[] s i: This can be interpreted as (1) = s[i] where =[] is the "fetch array element" operator. This part seems plausible.

    • (6) []= x (5): Here []= is the operator, x is the array, and (5) is the index. However, the index for x should be i, not the calculated RHS value (5). Using (5) as the index x[(5)] is incorrect based on the original expression x[i]. This definitively makes Option C incorrect.

Based on this detailed analysis, Option A consistently and correctly fills in the missing entries.

The final answer is $\boxed{A}$

questions.question_text:
Consider the following grammar (that admits a series of declarations, followed by expressions) and the associated syntax directed translation (SDT) actions, given as pseudo-code:

P → D* E*

D → int ID {record that ID.lexeme is of type int}

D → bool ID { record that ID.lexeme is of type bool}

E → E1 + E2 {check that E1.type = E2.type = int; set E.type := int}

E → !E1 {check that E1.type = bool; set E.type := bool}

E → ID {set E.type := int}

With respect to the above grammar; which one of the following choices is correct?

options.content: The actions will lead to infinite loop.
The actions can be used to correctly type-check any syntactically correct program.
The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct boolean variable declarations and boolean expressions.
The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct integer variable declarations and integer expressions.

questions.explanation:
To determine the correct option, we'll analyze the given grammar and its associated syntax-directed translation (SDT) actions, focusing on how they handle variable declarations and expressions.

Given Grammar and SDT Actions:

Grammar:

P → D* E*

A program P consists of zero or more declarations (D*) followed by zero or more expressions (E*).

D → int ID { record that ID.lexeme is of type int }

D → bool ID { record that ID.lexeme is of type bool }

Declarations D can declare variables of type int or bool.

E → E₁ + E₂ { check that E₁.type = E₂.type = int; set E.type := int }

E → !E₁ { check that E₁.type = bool; set E.type := bool }

E → ID { set E.type := int }

Expressions E can be additions, logical NOT operations, or identifiers.

SDT Actions:

In the action for E → ID, we have { set E.type := int }.

Issue Identified: This action sets E.type to int regardless of the actual type of ID.

Analysis of the Actions:

Declaration Handling:

Declarations correctly record the type of each ID in a symbol table.

int ID records ID as type int.

bool ID records ID as type bool.

Expression Handling:

Addition (E → E₁ + E₂):

Checks that both E₁.type and E₂.type are int.

Sets E.type to int.

Logical NOT (E → !E₁):

Checks that E₁.type is bool.

Sets E.type to bool.

Identifier (E → ID):

Problematic Action: Sets E.type to int without considering ID's actual type.

This means that even if ID is declared as bool, E.type will incorrectly be set to int.

Consequences of the Actions:

Integer Variables and Expressions:

For variables declared as int, the actions correctly set E.type to int.

The addition operation checks for int types and proceeds correctly.

Thus, integer variable declarations and integer expressions are correctly type-checked.

Boolean Variables and Expressions:

For variables declared as bool, the action E → ID { set E.type := int } incorrectly sets E.type to int.

When using a boolean variable in a logical NOT expression (!ID), the type check E₁.type = bool fails because E₁.type is incorrectly set to int.

Therefore, boolean variable declarations and expressions cannot be correctly type-checked with the given actions.

Evaluating the Options:

Option A: The actions will lead to infinite loop.

Incorrect: There is no indication of any looping behavior in the actions.

Option B: The actions can be used to correctly type-check any syntactically correct program.

Incorrect: The actions fail to correctly type-check programs involving boolean variables and expressions due to the issue with E → ID.

Option C: The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct boolean variable declarations and boolean expressions.

Incorrect: The actions incorrectly handle boolean variables in expressions, as they always set E.type to int.

Option D: The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct integer variable declarations and integer expressions.

Correct: The actions handle integer variable declarations and expressions properly, allowing for correct type-checking in these cases.

Final Answer:

Option D: The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct integer variable declarations and integer expressions.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following ANSI C program:

int main() {

Integer x;

return 0;

}

Which one of the following phases in a seven-phase C compiler will throw an error?
questions.explanation:
Given ANSI C Program:

int main() {

    Integer x;

    return 0;

}

Analysis of the Code:

Issue in the Code:

The line Integer x; is declaring a variable x with a type Integer.

In standard C, Integer is not a valid built-in data type. The correct keyword for declaring an integer variable is int.

Implication:

Using Integer as a type without prior definition leads to an error.

The compiler needs to detect that Integer is not a valid or declared type.

Compiler Phases and Their Functions:

A typical seven-phase compiler includes the following phases:

Lexical Analysis (Lexer):

Reads the source code character by character.

Groups characters into tokens (identifiers, keywords, operators, literals, etc.).

Example: Recognizes int, main, Integer, x, return, 0, etc., as tokens.

Syntax Analysis (Parser):

Takes tokens from the lexical analyzer.

Checks if the tokens form a valid grammatical structure according to the language's grammar (syntax rules).

Builds a parse tree representing the syntactic structure.

Semantic Analysis:

Uses the parse tree to identify the meaning of the code.

Performs type checking and ensures that all identifiers are declared before use.

Checks for semantic consistency (e.g., variable types, function calls with correct arguments).

Intermediate Code Generation:

Converts the parse tree into an intermediate representation (IR), such as three-address code.

This IR is a low-level code that is independent of the machine architecture.

Machine-Independent Optimization:

Performs optimizations on the intermediate code without considering the target machine architecture.

Examples include constant folding, dead code elimination, and loop optimization.

Code Generation:

Translates the optimized intermediate code into target machine code.

Allocates memory and registers, translates operations into machine instructions.

Machine-Dependent Optimization:

Performs optimizations specific to the target machine architecture.

Examples include instruction scheduling and register allocation optimizations.

Determining Which Phase Will Throw the Error:

Option D: Lexical Analyzer

Role:

The lexical analyzer tokenizes the input code.

It does not validate whether an identifier is a valid type.

In this code:

Integer is recognized as an identifier token.

No error is thrown at this phase.

Conclusion: Lexical analyzer will not throw an error.

Option A: Syntax Analyzer

Role:

The syntax analyzer checks if the sequence of tokens follows the grammatical rules of the language.

In this code:

The parser sees Integer x; as a declaration statement.

Syntactically, it's correct to declare a variable with an identifier as its type.

The parser assumes that Integer could be a valid type name (possibly defined elsewhere).

Conclusion: Syntax analyzer will not throw an error.

Option B: Semantic Analyzer

Role:

The semantic analyzer ensures that the code makes sense semantically.

It checks for:

Undeclared variables or types.

Type compatibility.

Correct use of operations on data types.

In this code:

Integer is used as a type but has not been declared or defined.

The semantic analyzer looks up Integer in the symbol table and fails to find it as a valid type.

This results in a semantic error: "Unknown type name 'Integer'".

Conclusion: Semantic analyzer will throw an error.

Option C: Machine-Dependent Optimizer

Role:

Optimizes the machine code considering the specific architecture.

Operates after code generation.

In this code:

Errors related to undeclared types would have been caught earlier.

The code would not reach this phase if semantic errors exist.

Conclusion: Machine-dependent optimizer will not throw an error in this scenario.

Final Answer:

The semantic analyzer is responsible for detecting undeclared or undefined types and variables.

Since Integer is not a valid or declared type in standard C, the semantic analyzer will report an error.

Answer: Option B — Semantic analyzer

questions.question_text:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.

(i) HTTP GET request for the index page

(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address

(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object

(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server

Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer?
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct chronological order of the packets leaving the user's computer, let's understand the sequence of events in a typical webpage loading process.

When a user starts browsing a webpage, the sequence of operations is as follows:

  1. First, the web browser needs to resolve the domain name of the web server into an IP address. Thus, the first packet sent will be the DNS request to resolve the web server's name.

  2. Once the IP address is resolved and received, the browser needs to establish a TCP connection with the web server. This is done by sending a TCP SYN packet to initiate the connection.

  3. With the TCP connection established, the browser can now send an HTTP GET request to fetch the index page.

  4. After receiving the index page, which contains references to multiple embedded image objects, the browser sends subsequent HTTP GET requests for each image object to the server.

Based on this logical sequence, the correct chronological order of the packets leaving the computer is:

Option C: (ii), (iv), (i), (iii)

Here’s the explanation of the sequence:

(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address: The first step is to find the IP address of the web server.

(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server: After knowing the IP address, the browser initiates a TCP connection with the server.

(i) HTTP GET request for the index page: With the TCP connection established, the browser requests the main index page of the website.

(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object: Once the index page is received, the browser then sends requests for various embedded image objects.

Suppose in a web browser, you click on the www.gate-2023.in URL. The browser cache is empty. The IP address for this URL is not cached in your local host, so a DNS lookup is triggered (by the local DNS server deployed on your local host) over the 3-tier DNS hierarchy in an iterative mode. No resource records are cached anywhere across all DNS servers.

Let RTT denote the round trip time between your local host and DNS servers in the DNS hierarchy. The group trip time between the local host and the web server hosting www.gate-2023.in is also equal to RTT. The HTML file associated with the URL is small enough to have negligible transmission time and negligible rendering time by your web browser, which references 10 equally small objects on the same web server.

Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed time between clicking on the URL and your browser fully rendering it?

options.content: 7 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
5 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
9 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
6 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.

questions.explanation:
Case I :

Persistent HTTP : TCP connection is established once and multiple files are transmitted in single connection.

Pipelined : New HTTP request can be sent to server without receiving acknowledgement of previous. $S_{a y}$ a client Alfiya request a page from server, following steps are followed in order before Alfiya gets all data needed :

(i) There's 3-tier DNS hierarchy, 100 kup is done in iterative mode taking 3 RTT.

(ii) 1 RTT is used for TCP connection establishment.

(iii) 1 RTT is used to fetch HTML base file.

(iv) 1 RTT is for all other 10 objects.

So, n total 6 RTT's are used.

Case-II : Non persistent HTTP with 5 parallel connections :

Non persistent : TCP connection is made for each HTTP request and closed.

5-prallel connections : 5 objects could be sent parallel at same time.

So, in this case the client Alfiya have to wait for request to be fulfilled as following steps need to be completed.

(i) 3 RTT for DNS resolution.

(ii) 1 RTT for TCP connection establishment.

questions.question_text: Consider the implementation of sliding window protocol over a lossless link, with a window size of $W$ frames, where each frame is of size 1000 bits (including header). The bandwidth of the link is $100 \mathrm{kbps}\left(1 \mathrm{k}=10^3\right)$ and the one-way propagation delay is 100 milliseconds. Assume that processing times at the sender and receiver are zero and the transmission time of acknowledgements is also zero. Which one of the following options gives the minimum size of $W$ (in number of frames) required to achieve $100 \%$ link utilization?
questions.explanation:
$$ \begin{aligned} \text { Window size } & =W \text { frames } \\ \text { Frame size } & =1000 \text { bits (Header + Data) } \\ \text { Bandwidth of link } & =100 \mathrm{kbps}, \text { Propagation delay = } 100 \text { millisec } \\ \% \mathrm{LU} & =100 \% \\ \end{aligned} $$

First, find the transmission time of one frame.

$$ \text {Transmission time } = \frac{\text{Frame size}}{\text{Bandwidth}} = \frac{1000}{100 \times 10^3} \text{ second} = 0.01 \text{ second} = 10 \text{ ms} $$

Now, use the NCERT-style relation for full link utilization in sliding window protocol:

$$ \text {Link Utilization} = W \times \frac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p} $$

For $100\%$ utilization, this value must be 1.

$$ 1 = W \times \frac{10}{10 + 2 \times 100} $$

Now simplify step by step.

$$ 1 = W \times \frac{10}{210} $$

$$ 210 = 10W $$

$$ W = 21 $$

So, the minimum window size required is:

$$ \Rightarrow \quad \text { Window size } = 21 $$

questions.question_text:
It is necessary to design a link-layer protocol between two hosts that are directly connected over a lossless link of length 3000 kilometers. Assume that the link bandwidth is $10^8$ bits per second and that the propagation delay in the link is 5 nanoseconds per meter. Every transmitted data byte is assigned a unique sequence number.

Let $N$ be the minimum number of bits needed for the sequence number field in the protocol header such that

(i) the sequence numbers do not wrap around before 60 seconds, and

(ii) the maximum utilization of the link is achieved.

The value of $N$ is $\_\_\_\_$ . (answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Given Data:

  • Link Length, $d = 3000 \text{ km} = 3000 \times 10^3 \text{ m} = 3 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$.

  • Link Bandwidth, $B = 10^8$ bits per second (bps).

  • Propagation delay per meter = $5 \text{ ns/m} = 5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s/m}$.

  • Every transmitted data byte is assigned a sequence number.

We need to find the minimum number of bits ($N$) for the sequence number field, considering two conditions. We will analyze each condition separately.

Condition (i): Sequence numbers do not wrap around before 60 seconds.

This condition relates the total number of sequence numbers to the rate at which they are used.

  1. Find the rate of sequence number consumption:

    The problem states that every byte gets a sequence number. So, the rate at which sequence numbers are used is equal to the rate at which bytes are transmitted.

    The bandwidth is given in bits per second. We convert this to bytes per second.

    Since $1 \text{ byte} = 8 \text{ bits}$,

    $$ \text{Rate of transmission} = \frac{\text{Bandwidth in bps}}{8} = \frac{10^8}{8} \text{ bytes/s} $$

    $$ \text{Rate of transmission} = 12,500,000 \text{ bytes/s} = 1.25 \times 10^7 \text{ bytes/s} $$

    This is the rate at which sequence numbers are consumed.

  2. Formulate the inequality:

    If we have $N$ bits for the sequence number field, the total number of unique sequence numbers we can have is $2^N$.

    The time it takes for these sequence numbers to wrap around ($T_{wrap}$) is:

    $$ T_{wrap} = \frac{\text{Total number of sequence numbers}}{\text{Rate of consumption}} $$

    $$ T_{wrap} = \frac{2^N}{1.25 \times 10^7} $$

    The condition is that this time must be at least 60 seconds.

    $$ \frac{2^N}{1.25 \times 10^7} \ge 60 $$

    $$ 2^N \ge 60 \times 1.25 \times 10^7 $$

    $$ 2^N \ge 75 \times 10^7 = 7.5 \times 10^8 $$

    This is our first requirement for the value of $2^N$.

Condition (ii): The maximum utilization of the link is achieved.

For maximum link utilization ($\eta = 1$), the sender must be able to send data continuously without waiting for an acknowledgment. This means the sender's window size must be large enough to "fill the pipe". The amount of data required to fill the pipe is called the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP).

  1. Calculate Propagation Time ($T_p$):

    This is the time it takes for a bit to travel from one end of the link to the other.

    $$ T_p = \text{Link Length} \times (\text{Delay per meter}) $$

    $$ T_p = (3 \times 10^6 \text{ m}) \times (5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s/m}) $$

    $$ T_p = 15 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s} = 0.015 \text{ s} $$

  2. Calculate Round Trip Time (RTT):

    RTT is the time for a signal to go from the sender to the receiver and a response to come back.

    $$ RTT = 2 \times T_p = 2 \times 0.015 \text{ s} = 0.03 \text{ s} $$

  3. Calculate the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP):

    BDP tells us the maximum number of bits that can be "in flight" on the link at any given time.

    $$ BDP = \text{Bandwidth} \times RTT $$

    $$ BDP = (10^8 \text{ bps}) \times (0.03 \text{ s}) = 3 \times 10^6 \text{ bits} $$

  4. Find the minimum number of sequence numbers for maximum utilization:

    To achieve maximum utilization, the sender's window must be large enough to hold at least BDP worth of data. Since each byte has a sequence number, we need to find the BDP in bytes.

    $$ \text{BDP in bytes} = \frac{3 \times 10^6 \text{ bits}}{8 \text{ bits/byte}} = 375,000 \text{ bytes} $$

    This means we need to have at least 375,000 unique sequence numbers available to assign to the bytes in the window. The total number of sequence numbers ($2^N$) must be at least this large.

    $$ 2^N \ge 375,000 $$

    This is our second requirement for the value of $2^N$.

Combining Both Conditions

Now we have two inequalities that must be satisfied:

  1. From Condition (i): $2^N \ge 7.5 \times 10^8$

  2. From Condition (ii): $2^N \ge 375,000$

To satisfy both conditions, we must choose the stricter (larger) one.

$$ 7.5 \times 10^8 \text{ is much larger than } 375,000 $$

So, we must satisfy:

$$ 2^N \ge 7.5 \times 10^8 $$

Now, we need to find the smallest integer $N$ that satisfies this inequality. We can use logarithms or check powers of 2.

We know that $2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$.

So, $2^{30} = (2^{10})^3 \approx (10^3)^3 = 10^9$.

Let's check the values around $N=30$:

  • For $N = 29$:

    $2^{29} = 2^{30} / 2 = 1,073,741,824 / 2 = 536,870,912 = 5.37 \times 10^8$.

    This value is less than $7.5 \times 10^8$. So, $N=29$ is not enough.

  • For $N = 30$:

    $2^{30} = 1,073,741,824 = 1.07 \times 10^9$.

    This value is greater than $7.5 \times 10^8$. So, $N=30$ is sufficient.

The smallest integer value of $N$ that satisfies the condition is 30.

The value of $N$ is 30.

questions.question_text: Suppose we are transmitting frames between two nodes using Stop-and-Wait protocol. The frame size is 3000 bits. The transmission rate of the channel is 2000 bps (bits/ second) and the propagation delay between the two nodes is 100 milliseconds. Assume that the processing times at the source and destination are negligible. Also, assume that the size of the acknowledgement packet is negligible. Which ONE of the following most accurately gives the channel utilization for the above scenario in percentage?
questions.explanation:
Let's break down the problem step by step:

Determine the transmission time for one frame:

The frame size is 3000 bits.

The transmission rate is 2000 bits per second (bps).

$$T_{transmission} = \frac{3000 \text{ bits}}{2000 \text{ bps}} = 1.5 \text{ seconds}$$

Consider the propagation delay:

The propagation delay between the two nodes is 100 milliseconds (0.1 seconds).

Since we're using the Stop-and-Wait protocol, the sender must wait for an acknowledgement, which will traverse back to the sender.

Assuming that the acknowledgement's transmission time is negligible, the total propagation delay (round-trip) is:

$$T_{propagation} = 0.1 \text{ seconds (forward)} + 0.1 \text{ seconds (backward)} = 0.2 \text{ seconds}$$

Calculate the total cycle time for one frame transmission:

$$T_{cycle} = T_{transmission} + T_{propagation} = 1.5 \text{ seconds} + 0.2 \text{ seconds} = 1.7 \text{ seconds}$$

Compute the channel utilization using the formula:

$$\text{Utilization} = \frac{T_{transmission}}{T_{cycle}} = \frac{1.5}{1.7} \approx 0.88235$$

Converting to a percentage:

$$0.88235 \times 100 \approx 88.23\%$$

Thus, the channel utilization for the given scenario is approximately 88.23%, making Option A the correct answer.

questions.question_text: Consider an Ethernet segment with a transmission speed of $10^8$ bits/sec and a maximum segment length of 500 meters. If the speed of propagation of the signal in the medium is $2 \times 10^8$ meters/sec, then the minimum frame size (in bits) required for collision detection is _________
questions.explanation:
To determine the minimum frame size required for collision detection in an Ethernet segment, we need to understand the concept of collision detection in the context of the CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) protocol used in Ethernet networks.

The key idea is that for a station to detect a collision, the frame transmission time must be at least twice the signal propagation time across the entire segment. This is to ensure that if a collision occurs, the transmitting station is still transmitting when the collision signal returns.

Let's break this down step by step:

Step 1: Calculate the signal propagation time

The maximum segment length is 500 meters, and the speed of signal propagation in the medium is $2 \times 10^8$ meters/sec. The propagation time ($t_{prop}$) can be calculated using the formula:

$$ t_{prop} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} $$

$$ t_{prop} = \frac{500}{2 \times 10^8} $$

$$ t_{prop} = 2.5 \times 10^{-6} \,\text{seconds} $$

Step 2: Calculate the round-trip propagation time

For collision detection, we need the round-trip propagation time, which is twice the one-way propagation time:

$$ t_{round-trip} = 2 \times t_{prop} $$

$$ t_{round-trip} = 2 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-6} $$

$$ t_{round-trip} = 5 \times 10^{-6} \,\text{seconds} $$

Step 3: Calculate the minimum frame size

The minimum frame size is determined by the amount of data that can be transmitted in this round-trip time. Given the transmission speed of $10^8$ bits/sec, the minimum frame size ($S$) in bits can be calculated using the formula:

$$ S = \text{transmission speed} \times t_{round-trip} $$

$$ S = 10^8 \times 5 \times 10^{-6} $$

$$ S = 500 \,\text{bits} $$

Therefore, the minimum frame size required for collision detection is 500 bits.

To find the correct values of $ x $ and $ y $ in the Hamming codeword, we'll use the properties of the Hamming code and the given bits.

Given:

Data bits:

Position Bit Value
d8 12 1

Position Bit Value

Parity Bit Calculations:

Parity bit $ c_1 $ at position 1:

Positions checked: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11

Bits: $ d_1 = 1 $, $ d_2 = 0 $, $ d_4 = 0 $, $ d_5 = x $, $ d_7 = 1 $

Parity equation:

$ c_1 + d_1 + d_2 + d_4 + d_5 + d_7 \equiv 0 \mod 2 $

Substitute known values:

$ 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + x + 1 \equiv 0 \mod 2 \implies (2 + x) \equiv 0 \mod 2 $

Solve for $ x $:

Parity bit $ c_2 $ at position 2:

Positions checked: 3, 6, 7, 10, 11

Substitute known values:

$ 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 \equiv 0 \mod 2 \implies (4) \equiv 0 \mod 2 $

Parity holds.

Positions checked: 9, 10, 11, 12

Parity equation:

$ c_8 + d_5 + d_6 + d_7 + d_8 \equiv 0 \mod 2 $

Substitute known values:

$ y + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 \equiv 0 \mod 2 \implies (y + 2) \equiv 0 \mod 2 $

Solve for $ y $:

$ y \equiv 0 \mod 2 \implies y = 0 $

Conclusion:

$ x = 0 $ and $ y = 0 $

questions.question_text:
Consider a simple communication system where multiple nodes are connected by a shared broadcast medium (like Ethernet or wireless). The nodes in the system use the following carrier-sense based medium access protocol. A node that receives a packet to transmit will carrier-sense the medium for $$5$$ units of time. If the node does not detect any other transmission in this duration, it starts transmitting its packet in the next time unit. If the node detects another transmission, it waits until this other transmission finishes, and then begins to carrier-sense for $$5$$ time units again. Once they start to transmit, nodes do not perform any collision detection and continue transmission even if a collision occurs. All transmissions last for $$20$$ units of time. Assume that the transmission signal travels at the speed of $$10$$ meters per unit time in the medium.

Assume that the system has two nodes $$P$$ and $$Q,$$ located at a distance $$d$$ meters from each other. $$P$$ starts transmitting a packet at time $$t=0$$ after successfully completing its carrier-sense phase. Node $$Q$$ has a packet to transmit at time $$t=0$$ and begins to carrier-sense the medium.

The maximum distance $$d$$ (in meters, rounded to the closest integer) that allows $$Q$$ to successfully avoid a collision between its proposed transmission and $$P’s$$ ongoing transmission is _____.
questions.explanation:
We have two nodes, $P$ and $Q$, separated by distance $d$ meters. The signal propagation speed in the shared medium is $10$ meters per unit time.

Node $P$ begins transmitting its packet at time $t=0$.

Node $Q$ also has a packet to transmit at $t=0$, so $Q$ starts carrier-sensing at $t=0$. By the problem statement, $Q$ will carrier-sense for $5$ time units.

If $Q$ does not detect any transmission during its 5 time units of carrier sense (i.e.\ in the interval $[0,5)$), it will begin its own transmission in the next time unit (i.e. at $t=5$).

If $Q$ does detect another transmission anytime in those 5 time units, $Q$ will refrain from transmitting at $t=5$ and will wait until that other transmission ends, and then re-sense again, etc.

Since $P$ is already transmitting from $t=0$ to $t=20$, the question is:

What is the largest distance $d$ between $P$ and $Q$ such that $Q$ still “hears” $P$’s transmission before $t=5$, and hence does not start transmitting at $t=5$?

Key Timing Condition

$P$ starts transmitting at $t=0$.

The signal from $P$ travels toward $Q$ at $10 \text{ m}\!/\!\text{(unit time)}.$

Hence, the time at which $P$’s signal first arrives at $Q$ is

$ \frac{d}{10} (\text{units of time}). $

For $Q$ to detect $P$ before finishing its 5 time units of carrier sensing (i.e. by $t=5$), we need

$ \frac{d}{10} \;\le\; 5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d \;\le\; 50 \text{ meters}. $

If $d > 50$, then $\frac{d}{10} > 5$, so $Q$ would not detect $P$’s signal before $t=5$. As a result, $Q$ would incorrectly conclude the medium is free and start transmitting at $t=5$, causing a collision.

Therefore, the maximum distance $d$ for which $Q$ still detects $P$’s ongoing transmission in time to avoid a collision is

$ d_{\max} = 50 \text{ meters}. $

The problem asks for the value rounded to the closest integer, which remains $50$.

Final Answer

$ \boxed{50} $

questions.question_text: An ISP having an address block 202.16.0.0/15 assigns a block of 6000 IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?
questions.explanation:
An ISP has the address block 202.16.0.0/15.

The client needs 6000 IP addresses.

In CIDR, the number of addresses in a block must be a power of 2.

The next power of 2 greater than 6000 is 8192.

Since $$8192 = 2^{13}$$, the block has 13 host bits.

So, the prefix length is $$32 - 13 = 19$$.

Hence, the client must be assigned a block of size $$/19$$.

Now we check which given blocks are valid $$/19$$ sub-blocks inside 202.16.0.0/15.

Given, Address block = 202.16.0.0/15

Client requires 6000 IP address [8192] 213 = 2 32 - 19

202.16.0.0

0001000.00000000.00000000

00010000.00011111.11111111

202.16.0.0/19

Option (a) is correct

202.17.64.0/19

00010001.01000000.00000000

00010001.01011111.11111111

Option (b) is correct

202.16.32.0/10

00010000.00100000.00000000

Option (c) is correct

202.17.24.0/19

00010001.00011000.00000000

Option (d) is false

For a $$/19$$ block, the third octet must increase in steps of 32, because $$256 - 224 = 32$$.

So valid network addresses can start with third octet values like 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160, 192, and 224.

Option (a): 202.16.0.0/19

This starts at third octet 0, which is a valid multiple of 32.

So this block is valid.

Option (b): 202.17.64.0/19

This starts at third octet 64, which is also a valid multiple of 32.

So this block is valid.

Option (c): 202.16.32.0/19

This starts at third octet 32, which is also a valid multiple of 32.

So this block is valid.

Option (d): 202.17.24.0/19

This starts at third octet 24, which is not a multiple of 32.

So this block is not a valid $$/19$$ network address.

Therefore, the possible blocks are (a), (b), and (c).

questions.question_text:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X .

Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X ?
questions.explanation:
The answer is Option D: Routing Information Protocol (RIP).

To explain briefly:

The IPv4 header’s protocol field indicates which protocol is carried in the payload of the datagram.

Both Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) and Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) are directly carried on top of IP, with protocol numbers 1 and 2 respectively.

Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is also a protocol that runs directly over IP (with protocol number 89).

RIP, on the other hand, is not directly encapsulated by IP. Instead, RIP messages are carried inside UDP datagrams (using UDP port 520). Hence, if an IPv4 datagram carries RIP data, its protocol field will indicate UDP (protocol number 17), not RIP.

That's why RIP is not a possible candidate for the value of the protocol field in an IPv4 header.

questions.question_text: Which of the following fields is/are modified in the IP header of a packet going out of a network address translation (NAT) device from an internal network to an external network?
questions.explanation:
When a packet goes out of a Network Address Translation (NAT) device from an internal network (private IP address range) to an external network (public IP address range), certain fields in the IP header are modified. Let’s examine each option to determine which fields are modified:

Option A: Source IP

Yes, the Source IP address is modified. NAT changes the source IP address from the private IP address of the internal network to the public IP address of the NAT device. This allows external devices to recognize and communicate back to the source device using the public IP address.

Option B: Destination IP

No, the Destination IP address is not changed by the NAT device when a packet is going out from the internal network to the external network. The destination remains the same as originally set by the internal device.

Option C: Header Checksum

Yes, the Header Checksum is modified. The IP header checksum is a value that is recalculated every time a change is made to the IP header (such as modifying the Source IP address). Since the NAT device changes the Source IP address, it must also recalculate and modify the Header Checksum to ensure data integrity.

Option D: Total Length

No, the Total Length field is not modified by the NAT device when the packet is sent out from the internal network to the external network. The total length field includes the header and the data section, and since the size of the packet remains the same, this value does not change.

In summary, the fields that are modified in the IP header of a packet going out of a NAT device from an internal network to an external network are:

Option A: Source IP and Option C: Header Checksum.

questions.question_text:
Consider a network path P—Q—R between nodes P and R via router Q. Node P sends a file of size $10^6$ bytes to R via this path by splitting the file into chunks of $10^3$ bytes each. Node P sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.

Each of the links P—Q and Q—R has a bandwidth of $10^6$ bits/sec, and negligible propagation latency. Router Q immediately transmits every packet it receives from P to R, with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router Q can simultaneously receive on link P—Q and transmit on link Q—R.

Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time $t = 0$.

Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which R receives all the chunks of the file?
questions.explanation:
Let's analyze the given problem step by step to calculate the time at which the last chunk of the file is received by node R.

We are given the following information:

  • File size = $$10^6$$ bytes
  • Chunk size = $$10^3$$ bytes
  • Bandwidth of both links P—Q and Q—R = $$10^6$$ bits/sec
  • Each byte is equal to 8 bits.
  • Negligible header size, propagation latency, processing, and queueing delays.

First, let's calculate the number of chunks:

Total chunks = $$\frac{10^6 \text{ bytes}}{10^3 \text{ bytes/chunk}} = 10^3 \text{ chunks}$$

Now, let's calculate the time required to send one chunk of size 1000 bytes from node P to router Q:

Size of each chunk in bits = $$10^3 \text{ bytes} \times 8 \text{ bits/byte} = 8 \times 10^3 \text{ bits}$$

Time to send one chunk over the link P—Q = $$\frac{8 \times 10^3 \text{ bits}}{10^6 \text{ bits/sec}} = 0.008 \text{ sec/chunk}$$

Since router Q can start transmitting the packet to R immediately after receiving it with no additional delay, we know that each chunk transmitted from P takes 0.008 seconds to reach Q and be sent out by Q.

We must account for the transmission time of the final chunk. The last of the 1000 chunks sent from P will finish reaching Q at:

The time to send 1000 chunks in series from P = $$10^3 \text{ chunks} \times 0.008 \text{ sec/chunk} = 8 \text{ seconds}$$

Finally, we need to add the time taken for router Q to transmit the last chunk to node R, which is the same 0.008 seconds:

Total time for the last chunk to reach R = $$8 \text{ sec} + 0.008 \text{ sec} = 8.008 \text{ sec}$$

So, the time at which node R receives all the chunks is:

Option B: 8.008 seconds
